planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, neutral to slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade, and shelter from cold, drying winter winds.

directions: This East Asian evergreen shrub forms a dense, horizontally branched mound of glossy, leathery, serrated leaves and performs best with a few hours of gentle morning sun followed by afternoon shade. Tiny, pendulous cream flowers hang beneath the branches in early-to-mid spring, and on female plants growing near a male they are followed by small, dusky-blue berries that ripen in fall. Give it rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil and protection from harsh winter wind, since foliage can suffer in exposed sites even within its hardiness range. It takes well to shearing and is often used as a low screening or foundation shrub beneath taller shade trees.
sources: NC State Extension Plant Toolbox - Eurya japonica

planting.note: Plant in spring in well-drained soil; naturally tolerant of salt spray and sandy coastal conditions, making it a candidate for Gulf Coast gardens in dappled shade.

directions: A compact relative of Japanese eurya, this evergreen shrub has shiny, shallowly notched leaves on yellow-brown stems and a naturally rounded, low-mounding habit. Sweetly scented, pale greenish-yellow flowers open in winter and are followed by decorative purple-black fruit. Native to rocky seashores of East Asia, it tolerates salt spray and sandy soil well and is traditionally used as a low hedge or windbreak near the coast. Grow it in well-drained soil with some shelter from the harshest afternoon sun for the glossiest foliage.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this hybrid will not come true from seed and is propagated only by cuttings.

directions: This intergeneric cross between Oregon grape (Mahonia aquifolium) and a barberry combines traits of both parents in one rounded evergreen shrub. New growth emerges in bronze and red tones before settling to glossy, spiny, holly-like leaflets, and clusters of small yellow flowers open in late winter to early spring. Black, berry-like fruit sometimes follows but is inconsistent from year to year. It is adaptable to most well-drained soils and, unlike many barberries, performs well in partial to full shade beneath larger shrubs or trees. Prune only to remove dead or crossing stems, since it blooms on old wood.
sources: NC State Extension Plant Toolbox - x Mahoberberis aquisargentii
Royal Horticultural Society - x Mahoberberis aquisargentii

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade; propagate by cuttings only, as this hybrid does not come true from seed.

directions: Discovered as a chance hybrid seedling at Miethke Nursery in Tacoma, Washington, growing among Oregon grape (Mahonia aquifolium), this evergreen shrub carries an unusual mix of foliage on the same plant, with some leaves showing the long spiny teeth of a Mahonia leaflet and others the shorter spines of its barberry parent. Small yellow flowers appear in spring, followed at times by black fruit that attracts birds. It is more shade-tolerant than most true barberries and works well as an understory accent or informal hedge in a woodland border. Site it in well-drained soil and avoid heavy pruning, which can spoil its naturally irregular, textural habit.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society) - x Mahoberberis miethkeana
Royal Horticultural Society - x Mahoberberis miethkeana

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in fertile, humus-rich, well-drained soil with consistent moisture, in part shade and a site sheltered from cold winter winds.

directions: Boxleaf azara is a South American evergreen grown chiefly for its late-winter flowers: tiny clusters of greenish-yellow stamens with no true petals, carrying a strong, vanilla-chocolate fragrance that drifts well beyond the plant itself. Small, glossy, box-like leaves give it a fine, airy texture, and the loose, fountain-like branching makes a graceful background shrub or small espaliered specimen against a sheltered wall. Flowers are occasionally followed by small berries, though fruiting is irregular. Grow in evenly moist, humus-rich soil in part shade, protected from harsh winter wind, which can damage foliage even within its hardiness range.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society) - Azara microphylla

planting.note: Plant in spring in organically rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in part to full shade.

directions: This Japanese woodland native forms a low, woody-based mound of large, softly textured, mint-scented leaves that brighten shaded borders through summer. In early fall it sends up dense, bottlebrush-like spikes of small pale flowers that are a late-season draw for pollinators when little else is blooming in the shade garden. It spreads gradually by rhizomes and self-layering stems to form a loose colony, making it useful as a textural groundcover beneath larger shade shrubs. Give it consistently moist, humus-rich soil, since leaves wilt quickly in dry spells, and cut the previous year's growth back in late winter.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Finder - Leucosceptrum japonicum
